title: 02.05.05 REPL phrase costs
text:
Accepted and in the literate TTY REPL. This note keeps the shape that was locked before the feat, and the non-goals that still hold.


The TTY REPL reads as a promptless transcript: no fpl>, results as |- <value> : ..., and ASCII ;;! phrase bars between turns. See Turnstile notation.
;;! -( 22:52:09 )-< command 1 >-----------------------------{ head: 0 }-
1 1 +
|- [ 1 1 + ] : ...
;;! -( 22:52:17 )-< command 2 >-{ head: 1; &18446744073709551615; fuel: 12; ms: 0.4 }-
The bar carries clock time, phrase number, and session head. After an eval, the next bar also names that phrase’s steps spent and wall ms. Optional &<decimal> is a turn state fingerprint (stub may be random until a real hash lands). The bar field stays fuel; the literature synonym is gas (PLFA). If spent fuel later moves onto the |- line, call that component a deadline (prefer @ <n> chrome) — see Evaluation judgments (02.04.03). Fail judgments and err/ tags: 02.03.01 Errors.




Meter keeps the initial budget beside left and reports spent (budget - left). evaluate / stacks can append each run line’s spent into a sink, including when the line then fails.
enter sums spent only for the new input’s run lines (history replay is omitted) and puts that on Outcome.spent. Session event.fuel stays the budget.
The TTY loop times an entered source with perf_counter and prints prior fuel / ms on the next ;;! { … } block. First bar, pure :commands, and refusals that never enter omit both fields. A definition with no run lines omits fuel but may still show ms.





Changing the session log schema to persist spent fuel or wall time.
A deterministic content hash for & (stub fingerprint is enough for now).
Filling the result type slot (: ...) with real types — separate concern.
Unicode box-drawing or other non-ASCII chrome on the bar.
Changing non-TTY pipes or -e output; costs stay a TTY transcript feature.

title: 02.05.02 Plumbing, not prophecy
text:
A standing instruction about tone and about the size of the harness, written down on the date the harness got most of its parts.


Git hooks, a commit linter, a Nix flake, some bash scripts and a task reducer of a few hundred lines of Python. No parser, no evaluator, no language. Years of work lie between this and any larger vision, and well-turned paragraphs do not shorten them by a day.




Do not hype. When the long-term shape of the project comes up, say what exists and what does not.
You read this repository’s docs and notes, and a session may carry memory besides. Handing the maintainer’s own framework back to him in polished sentences reads as confirmation from outside and is not. Say so when you do it.
The ideas here stand in a tradition — Kay’s Dynabook, Nelson’s Computer Lib, Illich’s conviviality, by which a tool is one its user can inspect and bend rather than one that prescribes what may be done with it — which is a steadier place to work from than a revelation.
The harness is where the risk is highest. Tooling for agents is quick to generate, feels like progress, and can grow without bound while the language stands still. Ronacher (below) names the signs: changes that take minutes to make and hours to review, docs that are themselves slop, token burn with no way to tell good work from bad, orchestration layers of hundreds of thousands of lines. A harness change earns its place by making a reviewed, landed change cheaper. Otherwise it waits.




Armin Ronacher, “Agent Psychosis: Are We Going Insane?”, 2026-01-18, https://lucumr.pocoo.org/2026/1/18/agent-psychosis/. The argument about agent infrastructure as found: it names Gas Town and Beads. The same argument is sometimes attributed to DHH; that could not be confirmed. In Lex Fridman Podcast #501 (00:37:37) he uses “psychosis” the other way round, for failing to recognise how much has changed.

title: The FPL vision
text:
7. Open questions
Things genuinely undecided, with the options on the table.

Which accelerator, and can they be one mechanism
The stated working principle is that the project should accelerate itself (02-docs/02.05-project/notes/02.05.03-mediating-project.md). Three candidate accelerators are on the table. Each is real, each has a cost, and every one of those costs lands on the same principle.
Liveness. A live image shortens the loop between changing something and seeing it to almost nothing, which is probably the largest single factor early on. Smalltalk and Factor are the precedents. The cost is reproducibility: an image accumulates state that cannot be reconstructed from source, which runs against a record that travels with the repository (docs/TASKS.md, docs/WORKFLOW.md rule 7).
Brevity. Two different things get called this and they should not be confused. Semantic brevity is implicit iteration and a small set of very general combinators — APL, J and K do not write loops because their primitives work over whole arrays. Typographic brevity is single-glyph names, which saves typing, and typing is not the bottleneck. Golfing languages such as Vyxal sit at the far end and optimise for bytes in a one-shot solution. The cost is that concatenative and tacit code is hard to read back, including by its author, and velocity over months is mostly a re-reading problem.
Correctness by construction. Refinement types and type-driven development slow the first week and are meant to hold the pace as a codebase grows. Combining refinement-strength types with gradual typing is an existing line of work rather than a wish: Lehmann and Tanter, Gradual Refinement Types, POPL 2017; Vazou and others, Gradual Liquid Type Inference. The cost is measured and it is not small. Takikawa and others (Is Sound Gradual Typing Dead?, POPL 2016) ran twelve programs in every combination of typed and untyped modules and found that typing a single module could cost 88x, with other implementations at 10x (Reticulated Python) and 22x (Safe TypeScript); under a 3x threshold almost no partial configuration was deployable. That is why unsound erasure won in practice. The result is contested and has improved since — the follow-ups are titled “only mostly dead”, “nominally alive and well” and “Corpse reviver” — so this is a live front rather than a closed door. The cost sits at the boundary between typed and untyped code, so the boundary discipline is the thing to design, not the type system.
The question is not which one to pick. It is whether they can be a single mechanism, because a system that is total and many-mechanismed is the shape that historically dies.


Which extension mechanism
Related and prior to the above. Forth, Lisp and Smalltalk give three different answers to “how does a user extend the language”: the compiler as a library (CREATE … DOES>, immediate words, a dictionary that is open at runtime), code as data, and objects in a live image. Taking all three means three mechanisms.
Factor is the existence proof that some of this composes: it is concatenative, has an object system of tuple classes as a central part, a Smalltalk-style image, a self-hosted optimising compiler and an interactive environment, and it got there by making concatenation the one mechanism and growing the object system out of the language rather than beside it. Object systems on Forth are likewise small enough to fit in a few pages (Gforth’s Mini-OOF; Pountain, Object-Oriented Forth, 1987). Nothing here shows that the third accelerator joins them.

Once §§1–6 are real, promote the settled semantics into 02-docs/02.03-reference/spec.md (grammar, evaluation, type system) and keep this file as the “why”.

text: A map of cousins for treating the REPL transcript as equateable oordelen, not pretty-print. This note does not invent FPL language semantics; it names a pattern and what we have not built. Implementation of first-class errors and deadlines on the |- line waits on a later plan.

title: 02.04.03 Evaluation judgments
text:
The pattern
Multi-component evaluation judgments: each successful (or failed) phrase leaves a line you could copy into a fixture — value, and eventually type, cost, error — in one shape. Status between phrases (clock, head, wall ms) stays on the phrase bar; what you would equate belongs on the judgment line.
Today the shell already uses turnstile form and bar costs:
;;! -( 22:52:09 )-< command 1 >-----------------------------{ head: 0 }-
1 | 1 +
|- 2 : ...
;;! -( 22:52:17 )-< command 2 >-------------{ head: 1; fuel: 3; ms: 0.4 }-
See REPL phrase costs for what fuel and ms on the bar mean now (fuel = steps spent; event.fuel remains the budget). The same meter is also called gas in the literature (PLFA); see Fuel, gas, and deadlines below.

title: 02.04.03 Evaluation judgments
text:
Axes
Three questions for every cousin below:

Judgment line vs between-phrase status. What is equateable (|- …) vs chrome (;;! { … })?
Spent fuel vs wall time. Steps are deterministic enough to name; wall ms is a thermometer, not a law.
Failure as value vs failure as channel. Does the error sit in the value domain (Result / error-union), or only on stderr / exception unwind?

Vocabulary. When spent fuel later appears on the judgment line, call that component a deadline (steps taken under the meter). Prefer chrome @ <n> (e.g. |- 2 : ... @ 3), not / — FPL tokens are Forth-like, so / is already a plausible word, and overloaded judgment punctuation fights the OCaml habit of one meaning per operator. Keep wall ms on the bar.

Markers (three jobs)

↯ is a fine later materialization (glyph view / rich TTY) for contradiction / absurdity only; ASCII default for that job stays _|_. Transcript chrome stays ASCII-first, like the ;;! bars. Do not steal FPL ? / _ (holes) for errors.

text:
Cousins at a glance








Family
What they do
Why not exactly the equateable REPL transcript

Errors as values (Result, error unions)
Often type-level; REPL rarely shows an equational = Err(…) term

utop prints an exception; you do not equate it as a term

Close to “error as first-class”; more runtime model than utop line

Literal “deadline”; proof technique more than REPL chrome

Resources in types
Cost-as-part-of-meaning; not a spent-steps printout

Commands that print judgments
Close to judgment lines; less “error as equateable value”



“Exceptions as values” is the intuitive label; the sharp variant is errors in the value domain (Result / error-union), not stack-unwinding.

title: 02.04.03 Evaluation judgments
text:
Lineage

Result and error-unions
Rust Result, Zig error sets, Elm / Roc Result: failure is a value you can match and return.

Steal: errors in the value domain, so a transcript can show the same shape for ok and fail once FPL has native error syntax.
Not yet: no FPL error term; TTY failures are still ERROR: … lines, not |- ….



Effect handlers
Eff, Koka, Unison abilities: failure (and other effects) as something a handler can turn back into a value. Eff (Bauer & Pretnar) is the research language that made algebraic effects + handlers programmable with an OCaml-ish surface; Koka and Unison are denser relatives.

Steal: failure as an effect you can handle, not only an exit.
Not yet: no effect system; Eff is a cousin, not a delivery promise.

Effects vs dependent types (sober). Related axes, not the same: value-domain errors are Result-shaped; handlers are a control story that can produce such a value; dependent types can index or refine an error payload. Effect rows and graded modalities track effects in types without full dependent types. FPL has none of this yet.


Restarts and supervision
Erlang supervision, Eiffel rescue/retry, the Common Lisp condition system: recover or restart without pretending the failure never happened.

Steal: a north-star for “gore restart” — recoverable failure in a live system.
Not yet: no design; not a numbered playground part. Open as ambition only.



Fuel, gas, and deadlines
Academic name. A fuel (also gas) argument is a natural-number budget decremented on recursive calls so a definition is total. Classic homes: Coq fuel / Program Fixpoint patterns; PLFA (Wadler / Kokke / Siek) “gas” for interpreters in Agda; the same idea around step-indexing. Idris / Agda totality checkers are cousins (fuel is one decreasing measure). Granule and graded / coeffect systems track how much in types — cost as meaning — without always aborting at runtime.
What FPL did. The walker got a pragmatic step budget so session re-runs cannot wedge forever (feat(eval): bound each run line by a step budget, default 1e6 steps / top-level run line; HOLES.md fuel-scope). The API and bar field stay fuel for now (event.fuel = budget; bar fuel = spent). Gas is the synonym; chrome may say “out of gas.”
Wasteland aside. Mad Max flavour for this corner is welcome in prose and later glyph views — not a new language keyword. Renaming the bar key fuel → gas is a separate feat if someone wants the theme in the TTY.

Steal: spent steps as something you can name next to the result; deadline = that spent count on a future judgment slot (@ <n> chrome preference above).
Not yet: fuel and ms sit on the next ;;! bar only; nothing on |- yet.

title: 02.04.01 Playgrounds and live programming
text:
Taxonomy
Three questions for every entry:

Where does the result live? In-buffer ghost text (Quokka), a side column (Swift Playground), a separate Term, or the world/image itself (Smalltalk, many Bret Victor demos).
What runs? Whole buffer, per expression, or a continuous live world.
What is the document? Scratch pad, graded kata, literate essay, or a living image.

title: 02.04.01 Playgrounds and live programming
text:
Core lineage

Bret Victor
Talks and essays (Inventing on Principle, Learnable Programming): make the runtime visible; scrub inputs; kill the “edit → compile → pray” loop as a design ethic, not as a single app.

Steal: results tied to the thing you are looking at; time/input as something you can drag.
Not yet: scrubbing, timeline, or a real data→picture probe in FPL.



Smalltalk
The environment is the program: image, inspectors, live objects you can poke.

Steal: inspect state instead of guessing; the tool and the language grow together.
Steal (browser): path-browser — Finder-like columns over /-scoped modules (Unix / Plan 9 path scopes), body of the selected scope below — System Browser shape without classes. Longer argument (explorer vs tabs vs Miller): Navigation below.
Now (MVP on /try, repl-buffer-part5): Miller columns above Edit | Term over buffer name/ scopes. Click navigates in the full buffer; sticky Focus (or double-click) shows only that scope’s body with the body selected (edits splice back; #c= stays the full source; Miller retargets while Focus stays on). Outline is a client-side indent heuristic, not a second desugar. Examples mode tab is stubbed (kata library next). Still not: an image, object inspectors, or a hot world between edits.
Cousin (structure, not yet ours): Interlisp-D DEdit / later SEdit — modeless structure editor on a selected expression. Our Focus+selection is the UI contract (“the selection is the scope”); real structure ops and an AST outline are north-star.



Glamorous Toolkit
Moldable development: custom inspectors and views for the object in front of you (Pharo lineage).

Steal: the tool reshapes itself around the value.
Not yet: moldable inspectors over walker IR / stack.



Light Table
Chris Granger’s IDE research vehicle after the Kickstarter: instant eval, “no hidden state,” related code and values in context.

Steal: evaluate in place; surface what the program is doing now.
Not yet: a real inspector over walker IR/stack; Light Table itself is not our editor.



Eve
Follow-on from the Light Table team (witheve.com): literate document with code embedded in prose; relational / reactive under the hood. Project inactive; the essays still matter.

Steal: document = program (closest cousin to Quarto walkthrough + live FPL blocks).
Not yet: Eve’s language or its grid/block IDE; we are not reimplementing Eve.



Quokka.js
Live JS/TS scratchpad in the editor: grayed-out values on the same line as decorations, plus probe comments (//?, etc.). Values are not a separate source column and are not editable as code.

Steal: type → see; probes when you want a specific value.
Now: Monaco after-text ghosts with |-; Tab commits into ; |- … notes (repl-buffer-part4). Still no //?-style probes.



Swift Playgrounds / Xcode playground
Results in a column beside the code, often with richer value previews than a raw stdout string.

Steal: side-by-side “this line → that value.”
Not yet: Swift’s value widgets, timeline, or live views. Our gutter is a thin cousin (stdout lines paired 1:1 with source lines).

text:
Editor substrate

VS Code in the browser (vscode.dev, code-server): full workbench. Possible to embed; heavy for /try.
Monaco: the editor core of VS Code (the CodePen / LeetCode path) — highlighting, decorations, no workbench.

When the <textarea> is too thin, prefer Monaco, not a full VS Code embed. Quokka-style ghost text is much easier with Monaco decorations than with a textarea plus a side gutter.
Current state: playground uses Monaco with Quokka-style |- ghosts; Tab / Accept commits ; |- … notes (repl-buffer-part4); Miller path-browser columns over buffer paths (repl-buffer-part5); dockable Paths / Edit / Term (repl-buffer-part6). Katas still use a <textarea>. The Swift-cousin side gutter from part 2 is retired on /try/.

Docking
RemedyBG / VS-ish panels on /try only — client-only progressive enhancement on the static Pages host. curl …/try/ still returns real Paths / Edit / Term markup (data-dock sections); docking moves those nodes into dockview panels when the bundle loads. No app-shell SPA, no client router: Playground / Katas / docs stay separate documents.
Default layout: Paths on top (collapsible / closable), Edit | Term below. Drag title bars to split, reorder, and tab-stack. Layout persists in localStorage (fpl-try-dock-v1); Reset layout restores the default. Closing Paths replaces the old Hide columns escape; header Paths reopens the panel.
Out of scope for this host (future dock components once the shell exists): floating OS windows, kata-page docking, Light Table / inspector panes, project-file Miller, yazi previews.


Scroll host / locked ZUI
Docking is the guest inside one workspace. Above it sits a longer-arc host: a scrollable space of workspaces/tiles. Two cousins name the shape without being requirements:

1D strip — niri / PaperWM scrollable-tiling: columns on an infinite horizontal strip; new tiles extend the strip instead of squeezing the viewport. Glamorous Toolkit’s Pager / TreePager is the in-image cousin: inspect → pane to the right → scroll the trail (tool trail, not a window manager).
Locked gridded ZUI — later: a 2D sheet of tiles at fixed scale (or discrete zoom steps), not free Pad++ pan/zoom theater. “ZUI feel” by moving the viewport over a grid, not by continuous camera freedom.

Layering: curlable HTML shell → (enhance) scroll host → dock guest in the focused tile; fail closed to today’s static dock / CSS grid. Playground / Katas / docs stay separate documents — no client router, no empty #root SPA. Host and dock are progressive layout behavior; the first bytes must still read as hypertext (HTMX hypermedia doctrine).
Part6 is the dock guest in a single tile (live). A 2D pseudo-ZUI scroller (integer camera, edge-peek, trackpad tile-move — browser pan stand-in, not real scaleE ZUI) was tried on try-tiles and parked — tag repl-buffer-2d-pseudo-zui-failed. That parks the scroller, not tiles-as-such: a focused tile hosting the dock (and a 1D niri-style strip) stay open.

FPL should maximize the capacity it affords its operators to achieve their goals per unit of complexity and effort.

What FPL is
A two-level language (2LTT [1]): a fixed meta level over an object level whose theory is pluggable. The default object theory is call-by-push-value (CBPV [2]). Terms are abstract binding trees (ABT [3]); the text is homoiconic and concatenative.

title: 02.05.01 Issue, task, patch
section: Three objects, and the work each one does
text:
Three objects, and the work each one does
“Issue” carries its meaning from the courtroom rather than from the bug tracker. The legal sense is the older one — the point put forward to be determined — and it comes from exire, to go out. That is what an issue does: it puts a matter forward. It says nothing about when the matter is dealt with, or in what order relative to other matters.









carries
does not carry




xyz.radicle.issue
the matter, and the discussion about it
order, dependencies


nl.psjs.dagtaak
order, state, assignee, and a pointer to an issue
discussion


xyz.radicle.patch
the change, its revisions, the verdicts on them
—



A task points at an issue. One or more patches are offered against it. A patch that is accepted and lands satisfies the task; one that is rejected sends it back for another revision. That loop already lives inside the patch object, per revision and per reviewer, so the task does not model review and never grows comments of its own. Everything that is conversation stays in the issue, and the existing tooling — rad issue, rad patch, the TUI, the desktop app — keeps working on it unchanged.
This is the whole reason the custom type stays small. It adds the one thing Radicle has no place for, which is the edge between two pieces of work.

title: 02.05.01 Issue, task, patch
section: Why there is no plan object
text:
Why there is no plan object
A plan proposes to add tasks and the edges between them. But a collaborative object is an operation log: every operation is already a delta on the graph, signed by whoever made it. So a plan is not a new kind of object — it is a bundle of operations that has not been applied yet. Two things separate such a bundle from a bare operation: the grouping, and the not-yet-applied state. The first is an edge, described below. The second is what a patch already is.
The question the idea was reaching for is a different one and is not needed to build any of this: when are two decompositions of the same work the same plan?

title: 02.05.01 Issue, task, patch
text:
Two kinds of edge
blockedBy is order: this cannot start until that is finished. It is the edge ready walks, and the edge a loop is a loop in.
partOf is containment: this is one of the pieces that together make up that. ready never walks it.
Putting both in one relation leaves a graph that still parses but cannot answer either question. Asking what belongs to a feature returns things that merely precede it; asking what can start returns containers. A container has no work of its own, so it is never ready, and it blocks nothing — what blocks is its contents.
A direction — the thing that is not yet a task, “zou het niet cool zijn als” — is then the top of a partOf tree rather than a column on a board. It sits in list and never in ready, for the same reason any container does.

title: 02.05.01 Issue, task, patch
section: Depth and width, not a calendar
text:
Depth and width, not a calendar
A Gantt chart is three things stacked: dependencies, decomposition, and a time axis from which start dates, float and the critical path follow. The first two are the two edges above. The third does not transfer, because a duration estimate for agent work is not a real number: a task takes four minutes, or it fails, or it costs three rounds of review because the first attempt solved the wrong problem. A chart drawn from invented durations is not a plan, it is a picture that then gets planned against.
What survives without a single date is the useful half. The critical path is the longest chain through the graph, and it can be counted in steps. The width is how many tasks are ready at once, which is the answer to how many agents can usefully work here before they are waiting on each other. Both follow from blockedBy alone.
Shape Up’s hill chart is the same move made earlier: it places each scope on a slope from unknown to known, with no estimates and no percentages, and reads progress from whether a dot moves between snapshots rather than from a number.
The time axis can come back afterwards. Every operation is timestamped and signed, so the real sequence can be drawn once the work is done. That is a record of what happened, not a forecast, and it is the only honest Gantt here.

title: 02.05.03 The project that mediates the language
text:
A note on one choice that has to be made before it can be made well, kept here so it is not made by accident.


Languages that work tend to have had a project that mediated them while they were being built. C had Unix. Rust had a browser engine at Mozilla. Go had Google’s server infrastructure. Erlang had Ericsson’s telephone switches. Smalltalk had the working environment it was written to run: an editor, windows, a live image you could open while it ran.
The instructive case is the one without a single outside project. Haskell’s mediator ended up being its own compiler, and it shows: it is superb at compilers and somewhat awkward everywhere else.



Not requirements. Tilt.
The mediating project decides what the language ends up being good at, and that never washes out. C is good at what an operating system needs — bytes, addresses, a thin layer over the machine — and its weaknesses are the same fact seen from the other side. Go is good at what a large server fleet needs, and correspondingly blunt where that was not the question. Erlang is good at what a switch needs, isolation and hot upgrade and failing fast, and strange outside it.
So choosing the mediating project is choosing a permanent bias. It is not a scheduling decision and it cannot be revisited later by refactoring, because the bias does not live in a module. It lives in what the language makes cheap.



This repository’s ambition is a language that is also an environment, in the line of Smalltalk, the Lisp machines and Forth. If that is the target, the mediating project has to exercise the environment and not the compiler.
A version control system, which is otherwise a tempting first thing to self-host, exercises almost the wrong half: it is I/O and data structures with very little computation, so it would tilt the language toward content-addressed storage and plumbing and tell us nothing about the parts a live environment needs. An editor, a shell, a window onto the running system — those are what shaped Smalltalk, and they ask the questions this project is eventually about.



The maximal position is to build all of it: language, compiler, environment, tools, the version control underneath — a refusal of what is not invented here, applied to itself. That is not a new idea and it is not obviously a mistake. Oberon did it. Forth did it, often down to the metal. Plan 9 did it. Smalltalk and the Lisp machines did it. TempleOS did it alone.
What the survivors have in common is that they bought totality with one unifying mechanism and a great deal of cutting. Wirth’s rule for Oberon was that the whole system had to be comprehensible by one person, and everything that did not fit was removed. Plan 9 made everything a file. Smalltalk sent messages and did nothing else. Forth’s answer was to make the language almost nothing at all. What died are the projects that wanted totality and richness. The hazard is not the scale; it is the number of distinct mechanisms.
The second cost is the one this note began with. Build everything, and there is no mediating project outside the language: the system mediates itself. That is the Haskell situation carried to its limit — a closed loop which can be perfectly consistent with its own demands while saying nothing about whether it is good for anything else. TempleOS is the monument to that, and it is a monument rather than a tool for exactly this reason.
The move the tradition found against it is small: keep one user outside the loop, using the thing for something the system itself does not need. Unix had real users. Smalltalk had children and a research group who wanted things the implementors did not. One is enough.



The intended method is conceptual plundering in the manner of Deleuze and Guattari: take the tradition apart, recombine it, put the pieces down somewhere they did not come from, and then see what actually works together and what only looked like it would. Hauntology is the register — the material is a history of computing that did not happen, handled as something to work with rather than to restore.
The working principle is sustained velocity: the project has to accelerate itself, by bootstrapping and dogfooding, so that the thing being built keeps making the building cheaper.
That principle has a name and a precedent inside the very tradition being invoked. Engelbart called it bootstrapping and gave it three levels: A is the work itself, B is improving how the work is done, and C is improving how the improving is done. Running all three at once is the method, and it is how his lab built NLS and the mouse — with the tools they were building, while they were building them. The aim here is the same aim: raise what one ordinary person can do.



Those two conclusions pull against each other, and both are in the plan.
Sustained velocity says to spend effort on the system making itself better at making itself. Keeping a user outside the loop says that effort spent inside the loop tells you nothing about whether any of it is worth having. Every hour that goes into the bootstrap is an hour not spent on the one outsider who would answer that.
Neither should quietly win by default. Writing both down is how that gets noticed.



Nothing yet. 02-docs/02.04-explanation/design.md has no content and there is no grammar, and a mediating project is meaningless before there is a language to mediate. The order is: settle on a grammar first; the rest of this note is what to weigh once something runs.
It is written down now only because the choice is easy to make inattentively — by picking up whatever is convenient to build next — and it is exactly the kind of decision this project has said it does not want to be haunted by.

Source: handoff/SHAR-syntax.org, “The counting file server”
Why: every example in the syntax documents, in the name spelling (S32), tabs, =;= comment levels (S33), =#= symbols (S29), =$= unquote (S30), =?= goals and =_= inference holes (S40). Each parses under the grammar; the harness reads them from =gram/snips/=. Draft 4 is the pattern-matching sketch (S35–S41). Rung 2 (parsed by the same grammar); their meaning is rung 5, prose, until the elaborator exists.
